housetrain.why: A puppy bladder physically holds roughly its age in months in hours. Accidents are biology plus missed timing.
fix: Out after every sleep, meal, play burst and roughly every 1 to 2 hours awake.
Reward the act outdoors within 2 seconds, treat at the spot, not back inside at the door.
Clean accidents with enzymatic cleaner, ordinary detergents leave scent invitations.
avoid: Never rub the nose in it or scold, the dog learns to hide peeing from you, hello behind-the-sofa puddles.
Do not free-roam an untrained puppy through the whole flat unsupervised.
housetrain.calm: Regressions around 4 to 6 months are textbook. Most dogs are reliable by 6 to 8 months, some honest souls take 12.

marking.why: Small, deliberate urine deposits on vertical spots, communication, not emptying. More common in intact males and in multi-dog homes.
fix: Rule out medical causes first, a urine test is cheap certainty.
Supervise, interrupt calmly mid-lift and head straight out, pay outdoor marking.
Enzymatic cleaning of every historical spot, old scent is an invitation.
avoid: Do not punish found marks, it increases sneaky marking.
Belly bands manage laundry, they do not train anything on their own.
marking.calm: Marking responds well to the supervise-clean-redirect triangle. Neutering reduces it in many but not all males, discuss timing with your vet.

heat.why: Females typically have their first heat between 6 and 15 months, small breeds earlier, large later. It lasts around 2 to 4 weeks with swelling, bloody discharge and behaviour changes. It is a normal, healthy cycle.
fix: Leash only for the whole heat, no dog parks and no off-leash, males detect it from kilometers away.
Hygiene pants for the flat help with discharge, most dogs also self-clean a lot.
Expect clinginess, moodiness or appetite dips, offer calm routines and patience.
Log the dates, cycles repeat roughly every 6 to 8 months, and discuss spay timing and options with your vet after the first heat.
avoid: Never leave her unattended in the garden, determined suitors climb fences.
Do not book training classes or dog gatherings mid-heat, it is unfair to everyone.
heat.calm: The first heat surprises almost every owner of a female puppy. Nothing is wrong with your dog, mark the calendar, manage 3 weeks, life resumes.

humping.why: Mostly over-arousal and stress relief, not dominance and often not sexual. Cushions, legs and dog friends are all targets.
fix: Interrupt calmly and redirect to a chew or a known cue like Place.
Spot the pattern: it usually spikes when excitement peaks, add calm breaks earlier.
If it targets one specific dog friend, give both more structured breaks in play.
avoid: Do not laugh and film it every time, attention feeds it.
Do not punish harshly, the underlying arousal needs an outlet, not a lid.
humping.calm: Embarrassing for owners, meaningless for dogs. Every dog owner has a humping story, ask any of them.

zoomies.why: Frenetic Random Activity Periods, sudden racing laps, are a normal energy release, classic after baths and in the evening.
fix: Let them run in a safe space, zoomies are healthy and self-limiting, usually under 5 minutes.
Move the party: open the garden door or clear the hallway of obstacles.
Frequent frantic zoomies can signal under-stimulation, add daytime sniffing and training.
avoid: Do not chase to stop it, you just joined the game.
No zoomies near stairs, slippery floors or roads, manage the terrain, not the joy.
zoomies.calm: Zoomies are one of the purest expressions of dog happiness. Enjoy the show, it is free entertainment.

begging.why: Those eyes once earned a chip. Dogs repeat what pays, dinner theatre included.
fix: Total embargo on table food from every family member, one leak funds the whole operation.
Give the dog a paid job at dinner: Place with a stuffed chew.
Pay the dog after dinner, away from the table, calm waiting earns the bonus.
avoid: No exceptions for guests or holidays, intermittent wins make begging bulletproof.
Do not shove the dog away repeatedly, boring consistency beats conflict.
begging.calm: With a true zero-payout policy, begging fades in a few weeks. The hard part is training the humans at the table.

stealing.why: Grab a sock, humans erupt into a chase, best game ever invented. Attention and play are the jackpot.
fix: Kill the chase: ignore low-value thefts completely, the game dies without a second player.
Trade calmly for real contraband, treat appears, sock drops, no drama.
Pre-load: more legal toys, more play initiated by you, fewer reasons to invoice you with socks.
avoid: Do not corner and grab, that builds guarding on top of stealing.
Do not chase around the coffee table, you are the entertainment.
stealing.calm: The sock thief phase is a rite of passage, especially with retrieving breeds. It fades once the chase economy collapses.

carfear.why: Motion sickness, or the car only ever drives to the vet. Both create bad math about cars.
fix: Rebuild in steps: meals near the parked car, then in it, engine off, then engine on, then 100 m drives.
Drive to great places: 5 minutes to the meadow, party, home.
For drooling and vomiting, ask the vet about motion sickness treatment, puppies often outgrow it.
avoid: Do not force a trembling dog in and drive off, each flooded ride deepens it.
Do not feed a full meal right before early practice drives.
carfear.calm: Very common, very fixable. Many former car-haters end up sleeping through highway trips within a couple of months.

greetpee.why: Young dogs have immature bladder control, big greetings overflow it. Submissive peeing is a related appeasement signal, not spite.
fix: Make arrivals boring: no eye contact, low voice, greet after 2 minutes outside if possible.
Greet crouched sideways instead of looming over the puppy.
Confidence work helps the submissive type: reward-based training, no scolding.
avoid: Never punish it, punishment increases submissive peeing directly.
Do not let guests squeal over the puppy at the door, brief them first.
greetpee.calm: The majority of puppies simply outgrow this by 12 months as the bladder matures. Manage the entrance hall, not the dog.

nailfear.why: Paws are sensitive, clippers are weird, and one painful quick-cut can create a long memory.
fix: Break it down: touch paw, treat. Hold paw, treat. Clipper appears, treat. Clipper touches, treat. One nail, jackpot. Days per step is fine.
One nail a day is a perfectly respectable pace.
A scratch board (sandpaper on wood) lets the dog file its own front nails as a trick.
avoid: Do not pin the dog down for a full pedicure, you buy 1 session and pay with 50.
Do not cut into the quick in dark nails, trim tiny slivers.
nailfear.calm: Nail fear is one of the most common handling issues. The cooperative-care approach works, thousands of scratch-board dogs prove it.

brush.note: Coated breeds: daily. Ask a groomer which tool.

vetkit.note: Tick remover, dog nail clippers, dog-safe shampoo.

dental.note: Enzymatic dog toothpaste only, never human paste. Daily is ideal, 3 times a week is real life.

longline.note: The recall training bridge to off-leash.

whistle.note: Consistent sound, carries further than voice.

raincoat.note: Some dogs need it, many do not.

gps.note: Peace of mind for off-leash phases.

agility.note: Garden fun once the dog is grown.

pros: Light and simple, carries the ID tag
cons: All pressure lands on the throat
Risky for pullers: trachea, thyroid and neck strain
Some dogs slip out of loose collars
collar.verdict: Keep it on for the ID tag. Walk on it only if the leash stays loose.

pros: Pressure on the chest and shoulders, not the throat
Best default for puppies and training
cons: Fitting matters, straps must not cut across shoulder movement
A badly designed harness can rub armpits
yharness.verdict: Opinion: the right default for most dogs. Y-shape on the chest, 2 fingers of slack everywhere.

pros: Turns the dog toward you when pulling, mechanics help retraining
cons: A tool, not a cure, training still required
Constant front-clip walking can affect gait, use during retraining
frontclip.verdict: Good temporary aid for strong pullers alongside loose-leash training.

cons: Short radius for sniffing on rural walks

pros: The recall and off-leash training tool
cons: Needs open space and some handling skill

pros: Convenient radius for trained, calm dogs in open areas
cons: Teaches pulling, tension extends the range
Cord injuries to human and dog are documented
No control in sudden traffic situations
Banned or frowned upon in many training schools

pros: Fast for quick transfers, common at vets and shelters
cons: Tightens on the neck without limit
Wrong tool for pullers and for daily walks
slip.verdict: Professional short-transfer tool, not a daily walking leash.

body: Size: pea-sized or smaller. A 5-minute session can burn 30 treats, small keeps the calorie math sane.
Soft beats crunchy, chewing pauses kill training rhythm.
Build a value menu: kibble for easy jobs at home, cheese, chicken or sausage for recall and hard outdoor work.
Take treats out of the daily food ration, training calories count too. Rule of thumb: treats within about 10% of daily intake.
Toxic and off-limits: chocolate, grapes and raisins, onion, garlic, xylitol sweetener, alcohol, cooked bones.
A clicker is a precision instrument: the click marks the exact moment the dog earned the reward.
Charging it: click, then treat, 10 to 15 times, until the click makes the ears perk. That is the whole setup.
The contract: every click is always paid. No exceptions, or the instrument loses value.
Click timing beats treat timing, the treat can arrive 2 seconds later, the click cannot.
No clicker at hand: a short marker word like Yes, said the same way every time, does the same job slightly less precisely.
Weeks 3 to 6: 28 baby teeth arrive.
Months 3 to 7: baby teeth fall out, 42 adult teeth erupt. Peak chewing pressure, sore gums, occasional blood spots on toys, all normal.
Relief menu: rubber chews, a wet frozen washcloth, frozen carrot pieces under supervision, and coffee tree or olive wood chews, which crumble instead of splintering like garden sticks.
Check occasionally for retained baby teeth, a double row of fangs needs a vet look, common in small breeds.
By month 7 the storm is mostly over. Protect cables and shoes until then, not forever.
Puppies need 16 to 20 hours of sleep per day. Most biting, zoomie and whining meltdowns are simply an overtired puppy past its bedtime.
Build a nap rhythm: roughly 1 hour awake, then a nap, for young puppies. Play, potty, then into the safe space for sleep.
Enforce naps in a calm, dim spot, a covered crate or pen works. An overtired puppy often cannot fall asleep alone in the middle of household action.
Protect night sleep: last potty late in the evening, then boring darkness. Young puppies may need 1 night toilet trip, keep it silent and businesslike.
If the puppy turns into a landshark, do not train through it. It is nap time, not discipline time.

homeguide.n: First days in the new home
body: Shrink the world: 1 room plus the safe space for the first days. The whole flat is earned gradually, room by room, it keeps toileting and chewing manageable.
Set up a base: bed or crate, water, a chew, in a corner where the puppy can see you but rest undisturbed. This is the retreat, never the punishment spot.
First night: sleeping distance matters. Many puppies settle faster next to the bed for the first nights, you can migrate the bed later.
Keep the first week boring on purpose: no visitor parades, no puppy parties. The puppy is processing losing its litter, the household is enough excitement.
Start routines from day 1: same feeding times, same potty door, same words. Predictability is how a puppy learns the world is safe.
Roughly 3 to 14 weeks of age is the period when puppies file experiences as normal. What is calmly met now is boring for life, what is missed can need real work later.
Socialisation means calm exposure, not maximum contact. Watching a bus from 30 meters while eating treats is perfect socialisation, being mobbed by 5 dogs is not.

Work a checklist: surfaces (grass, metal grates, stairs), sounds (traffic, vacuum, thunder recordings at low volume), people (hats, beards, wheelchairs, children at distance), handling (paws, ears, mouth).
Before full vaccination: carry the puppy through busy places, visit vaccinated friend dogs at home, sit on a bench near life. Exposure does not require pavement contact.
One rule above all: the puppy sets the pace. Forced greetings teach fear, voluntary approach teaches confidence.
Being alone is a skill, not a default. Puppies that never practice it become dogs that panic, start with seconds, not hours.
Day 1: step out of the room for 10 seconds while the puppy eats from a food toy, return before any fuss. That is a rep.
Grow slowly: seconds to minutes to a quiet coffee outside the door. Leave a stuffed chew, keep departures and returns completely boring, no dramatic goodbyes.
Aim for a puppy that can nap alone for 30 to 60 minutes within the first weeks, always after exercise, potty and with something to chew.
If the puppy panics rather than protests, do not push through the crying, shrink the step. Real separation distress deserves a professional plan early, it does not fix itself.

walksguide.n: Puppy walks: how long, how often
body: Rule of thumb: about 5 minutes of structured walking per month of age, 1 to 2 times a day. A 4-month puppy: around 20 minutes per walk.
This caps forced marching, not movement. Free play, sniffing and soft-ground time regulate themselves.
Sniffing IS the walk. A slow 20-minute sniffing tour tires a puppy more than 40 brisk minutes.
Growing joints dislike long hikes, stair marathons, jumps from height and running on asphalt. Save jogging and bike training for 12 to 18 months.
Watch the puppy, not the clock: lagging, lying down or frantic biting mid-walk means it was too much. Carry a small puppy home rather than dragging it.
3 to 4 short outings beat 1 long one, and every outing doubles as toilet training.
Timing: first heat between 6 and 15 months, small breeds earlier, large breeds later. It repeats roughly every 6 to 8 months.
Duration: around 2 to 4 weeks. Signs: swollen vulva, bloody discharge, more frequent peeing, mood swings, magnetic attractiveness to every male in the postcode.
Management: leash only for the full duration, no dog parks, no unattended garden time, hygiene pants indoors if needed.
She may be clingy, tired or picky with food. All normal, keep routines calm.
After the first heat, discuss spaying pros, cons and timing with your vet. There are real arguments on both sides and breed size matters, it is a personal decision, not a default.
Log the dates in your calendar. Predictability makes round 2 easy.

items: Test the basics honestly: sit, down, stay, recall, each in the living room and in the garden
Re-train anything shaky with 3-minute sessions, no shame, rust is normal
Pick your reward currency: which treat makes your dog's eyes light up
planAdult.note: Do not assume anything is solid. Testing honestly this week saves 6 weeks of frustration later.

items: Loose leash walking, 10 minutes daily on a quiet route
The stop-when-it-tightens rule, every single time
Sniffing breaks on cue as the walk's salary
planAdult.note: Loose lead is a habit, not a trick. Consistency beats intensity every single time.

items: Leave it, from floor food to dropped food
Wait at doors and before the food bowl
Stay: grow duration to 30 seconds with you stepping away
planAdult.note: Recall is a life skill. Never call your dog to end something fun, or the cue starts to mean the fun stops.

items: Settle on a mat during dinner and TV evenings
Calm behaviour gets quiet payment, chaos gets nothing
First cafe rehearsal at home: mat, chew, 20 minutes
planAdult.note: Settle work looks like doing nothing. It is the single most useful thing an adult dog can learn.

items: Recall on a long line in the park, pay like a lottery win
Add distractions gradually: distance from other dogs, then closer
Emergency stop cue as a separate skill
planAdult.note: Impulse control is built in seconds, not minutes. Short reps, high value, walk away winning.

items: Chin rest for husbandry: ears, eyes, paws
Teeth brushing 3 times this week
Nail trim or grinder session, 1 paw at a time
planAdult.note: Distraction is the real test. Drop your criteria in a new place, that is not backsliding, that is training.

items: Cafe or restaurant visit for real, short and successful
Polite greetings: sit to say hello, no jumping
Waiting calmly while you chat with someone on the street
planAdult.note: Adult dogs learn tricks faster than puppies. Use them to rebuild confidence after a hard week.

items: Scent games: find-the-treat around the flat and garden
Teach 1 pure fun trick as a reward for you both
Review week: retest week 1, celebrate the difference, plan what is next
planAdult.note: Maintenance beats perfection. 5 minutes on 5 days a week keeps everything you have built.

items: Name recognition
Charge your marker word or clicker
House-training rhythm, out every 1 to 2 hours
planPup.note: No commands pressure this week. Bonding, sleep and toilet timing are the curriculum.

items: Sit, 3 short sessions a day
Keep paying name recognition
Crate games with the door open
planPup.note: 3 minutes counts as a session. Short and happy beats long and tense.

items: Down
Review Sit in new rooms
Handling: touch paws and ears, pay each touch
planPup.note: If Down is not smooth by Sunday, that is fine. Carry it into next week.

items: Come indoors, hallway ping-pong
Review week: Sit and Down before meals
Wait at the food bowl, 2 seconds
planPup.note: Recall is a marathon skill. Indoors only for now.

items: Leave it, basic fist game
Drop it during play
Keep paying indoor recall
planPup.note: Half of dog training is teaching the dog that giving up pays better than grabbing.

items: Loose leash, first 100 slack meters
Watch me on the street
Sit at 1 curb per walk
planPup.note: Pulling is normal at this age. Stop-and-go, no yanking, tiny distances.

items: Stay, 1 to 5 seconds duration only
Place on the mat
Review recall, now with mild distractions
planPup.note: Seconds, not minutes. Breaking a stay twice in a row means make it easier.

items: No new skills
Mixed 5-minute review sessions of everything
1 fun trick of your choice as dessert
planPup.note: Review weeks are progress. A skill is only real once it survives a week of mixed practice.

items: Wait at the curb, every crossing
Loose leash on busier streets
Calm visitor routine, first setups
planPup.note: The world is the classroom now. Shorter routes at higher quality beat long marches.

items: Stay with 2 to 5 steps of distance
Recall outdoors on the long line
Down on the mat while you cook
planPup.note: If any skill wobbles, drop back a week. The calendar serves you, not the other way around.

items: Settle under the table, first cafe visit
First calm car rides
Vet-style handling: paws, ears, teeth check
planPup.note: These are the skills that make the next 10 years easy. Worth every rep.

items: No new skills
Mixed 5-minute reviews of the whole toolbox
1 favourite trick, polished for show
planPup.note: 12 weeks in: you have a trained young dog and a daily habit. The habit is the real graduation gift.

cmd: Lure every rep with a treat in your hand, reward within 1 second. Success = the behaviour happened at all, with your full help.
Sessions 2 to 4 · Lure and name it
Keep luring, say the cue once just before the behaviour. Success = 3 to 5 helped reps in a row.
Empty hand, same motion, reward from the pouch. Positions earn 1 to 3 seconds of waiting before the pay.
One cue, no lure. Grow one difficulty at a time: duration past 5 seconds, new rooms, mild distraction.
trick: Big obvious lure, instant pay for any movement in the right direction. Success = a rough version happened once.
Pay the best 3 of 5 attempts, ignore the rest. Say the cue once per rep. Keep sets to 3 to 5 reps, tricks tire the brain.
The lure becomes a small hand signal. Precision rises: the cleanest reps earn a double treat.
Cue first, hand signal only as backup. New rooms, then in front of people. Applause counts as distraction.
agi: Bar on the ground, tunnel short, table low. Success = 1 happy attempt, paid like a jackpot.
Sessions 2 to 4 · Build love, not height
Repeat the easy version until the dog drags you toward the obstacle. Confidence first, criteria later.
Height, length or angle, never two in one session. Say the obstacle cue as the dog commits.
Session 8 and on · Speed and sequence
Send from a few steps back, chain 2 obstacles, keep sessions under 10 minutes. Joy is the engine of agility.
life: Short and easy version, below the point of stress. Success = calm moments in the situation, then leaving on a good note.
Outings 2 to 4 · Distance is your dial
Repeat at a distance or duration where the dog can still eat, sniff and look at you. Pay calm constantly.
Closer, longer or busier, one knob per outing. Retreating is a strategy, not a failure.
Outing 8 and on · Make it routine
Vary days, places and times so the calm generalises. A 5 means relaxed from arrival to exit.

stucks.cmd: Stuck? Make it easier, not louder. Go back one step, collect 2 easy wins, end there. Show again with a lure instead of repeating the cue. If the dog stands up from a position, reward faster next rep.
stucks.trick: Stuck? Split the trick into smaller pieces and pay the smallest one. Film a session, most trick problems hide in the human hand, not in the dog.
stucks.agi: Refusing the obstacle? Lower it, shorten it, or go back to paying mere attempts. Never push or lift the dog onto equipment, one scared rep costs weeks.
stucks.life: Overwhelmed rather than stuck? Add distance, shorten the outing, end on calm and try again another day. Exposure work fails loudly but recovers quickly.
